Chapter 06INPUT

The Old Line

On wet nights the puddles show rails the street no longer has.

Vancouver has taken a lot of routes off its maps: streetcar rails, rail spurs, stops that used to matter. On wet nights they come back. Look into a puddle on a street with no tracks and you may see rails shining in the reflection. This is the Old Line. It does not run on a timetable and it does not care what the current map says; old alignments and old versions of a corner are all still there under the asphalt, all still in use. The Freight shares its rails but does the opposite job: the Freight removes what cannot stay, and the Old Line keeps what must not be forgotten.

The Old One stops the cart beside a puddle. On the dry road, a truck is reversing. In the puddle, rails run beneath it and turn toward the back of the new development.

The Kid crouches to look. The rails disappear when a tyre breaks the water, then return. The Kid points along the reflected track. “Shortcut?”

“Once,” says the Old One, already pushing the cart around the long way. The Kid looks from the rails to the brick wall in their path, then follows with the skateboard under one arm.

Vancouver has removed plenty of routes from its maps. The Repair People can still follow them. The Old Line keeps the ways people used to move, and the places they once had reasons to stop. Its rails do not promise to take anyone where a current map says they should go.

At the rear of the courtyard, another puddle briefly holds the reflection of an open doorway. Above it stands the same doorway bricked shut. There is no ghost waiting inside. The Old One looks from its worn threshold to the unused new bench.

On the back of a scrap of paper, the Kid draws the curve of the reflected rail. The Old One taps the near end, then points toward the courtyard entrance.

They take the drawing to the bench painter. The old route will not be rebuilt as track. A line of paint can still help a person find somewhere to stop.

The ruleYou may follow an old route. You may not assume it goes where the current map says.

Terminal City is an original fictional mythology inspired by Vancouver’s geography, weather, wildlife, infrastructure, art, and electronic music. It makes no claim to historical, Indigenous, or religious tradition. Real places are used as settings; the operating system layered on them is invented.
Made by Steve Hiehn, a software developer and electronic musician based in Vancouver, Canada. All music was created using a custom DAW, Signals & Sorcery.
